objectives: Secure the tube and check it for displacement and skin damage.
Care for the inner cannula, humidification, cuff and stoma as the unit's protocol directs.
Suction only when needed and recognise the difficult catheter pass as an emergency.
Recognise the red flags of a tracheostomy problem and use the bedhead sign and emergency algorithm.

items.text: Patients with a tracheostomy often need suctioning to keep the airway open, and each patient needs individual assessment and constant reassessment of how often.

An inadequately secured tube may become partly or completely displaced and obstruct the airway; consider partial displacement whenever the patient deteriorates or becomes distressed, because it may not be obvious.

Tracheostomy and laryngectomy patients have different airflow routes and are managed differently in an emergency: a patient with a laryngectomy cannot be ventilated through the nose and mouth and must be ventilated through the stoma.
Any difficulty passing a suction catheter should raise the possibility of a partly blocked, badly orientated or misplaced tube and needs immediate attention as an emergency.
Transfers between areas of patients with tracheostomies must be planned between the nursing and medical staff of both areas because unfamiliarity is a clinical risk.

Assess for secretion accumulation and obstruction. Follow the specific inner cannula manufacturer's instructions and local cleaning or replacement policy; a single-use inner cannula must not be cleaned for reuse. Check and document patency and care as indicated, rather than applying one cleaning interval to every tube.

Check securement against the specific holder or tube instructions and local policy, assess for pressure injury and obtain trained assistance for holder adjustments where dislodgement is a risk. The one-finger tape check in the older NHS board guidance is not a universal rule.
Keep a spare inner cannula in a clean container at the bedside; some tube makers require the inner cannula in place before connecting oxygen, a circuit or a bag-valve device.

An AARC clinical practice guideline panel found evidence supporting three system-level approaches to adult tracheostomy care in the acute care setting: using a tracheostomy bundle that a team of subject-matter experts has evaluated and endorsed; adding a multidisciplinary tracheostomy team to the management strategy; and following a protocol to guide weaning and removal of the tracheostomy tube. These are organisational and team-based recommendations, not a specific bundle, team composition or weaning protocol; the unit's own protocol and team structure govern.
Who may change tubes, deflate cuffs, decannulate and suction a tracheostomy follows local policy and competence; this guideline expects staff caring for these patients to have the required training.

An emergency box stays with the patient, including during transfers, with a spare tube and inner cannula (same size and a smaller size), dilators, a means of securing the tube, suction catheters, a syringe for cuffed tubes and oxygen masks; a cuff manometer, humidification spares and the correct bedhead sign with the emergency algorithm belong at the bedside.
For a transfer, take tracheostomy spares in line with the National Tracheostomy Safety Project (ICS 2026 recommendation 60).
Humidification must match the patient's condition and secretions, using a ladder of devices, and saline nebulisers or mucolytics and hydration are considered if secretions are not improving.

Inspect the stoma daily for signs of infection; keep it clean and dry; routine dressings are not recommended, and any dressing must be pre-cut and made for tracheostomy use so fibres do not enter the airway.

Suction when necessary, encouraging deep breaths and coughing first; the guideline gives example indications (noisy breathing, ineffective cough, visible or audible secretions, increased work of breathing, falling saturations) and lists the risks (hypoxia, mucosal trauma, arrhythmia, atelectasis, bronchospasm, infection, bleeding, raised intracranial pressure, interruption of ventilation).

If a fenestrated tube is in place, change to a non-fenestrated inner cannula before suctioning; this guideline states a catheter no wider than half the inner lumen, suction not longer than about ten seconds and a stated vacuum range (local guideline values; the unit's protocol governs).

Cuff pressure is checked with a manometer; this guideline cites a recommended range and twice-daily checks unless more are indicated (local guideline values), and warns that too low a pressure causes a leak and micro-aspiration while over-inflation impairs tracheal blood flow.

Red flags: for a correctly sited cuffed tube no air should escape through the mouth (talking, audible leaks or bubbling saliva suggest a cuff or placement problem); apnoea on capnography, difficulty breathing, higher airway pressures, lower tidal volumes, hypoxia and noisy breathing; a visibly displaced tube, blood around the tube, new pain, or needing a lot of air to keep the cuff inflated; and any change in respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure or consciousness, including anxiety, restlessness or confusion.

Suspected obstruction or displacement, including inability to pass a suction catheter, requires immediate airway-emergency escalation; do not wait until peri-arrest. Use the patient-specific tracheostomy or laryngectomy emergency pathway and obtain trained assistance. Avoid forcing a catheter or ventilation through a potentially displaced tube; follow the trained team's airway assessment and capnography pathway.
Risks include displacement and obstruction, bleeding, stoma skin irritation or infection, cuff-related tracheal injury and, with a low cuff pressure, aspiration and pneumonia.
Record safety checks, suction, oxygen and inner-cannula care on the unit's tracheostomy chart; document and explain any inner cannula that is not changed.
Plan transfers with the receiving team, and keep the bedhead sign and emergency algorithm with the patient.

checklist.text: Confirm the bedhead sign, emergency box, suction, oxygen and spare tube are at the bedside.
Check securement according to the tube/holder instructions and local procedure; assess the neck for pressure injury and seek trained help if displacement is suspected.
Look and listen for red flags: air leak at the mouth, noisy breathing, displaced tube, blood around the tube, new pain.
Check inner-cannula patency; clean reusable or replace single-use components according to the device instructions and local policy.
Suction only when needed; if the catheter will not pass, treat it as an emergency and call for help.
Check cuff pressure with a manometer at the unit's interval.
Inspect the stoma daily and keep it clean and dry.
Activate the airway emergency team immediately for suspected blockage or displacement, including inability to pass a suction catheter; follow the patient-specific emergency pathway.
Record checks and care on the tracheostomy chart.

gaps: The guideline is one NHS board's document, past its review date (November 2024); numerical values (cleaning interval, cuff range, suction duration and vacuum) are marked partial and unit policy governs.

The NTSP algorithms themselves, which the guideline reproduces with permission, were not read from the NTSP; the AARC 2021 CPG's three system-level recommendations were read, but its full literature-review tables and individual cited studies were not; the NSW ACI guide and the Open RN chapters remain genuinely inaccessible (HTTP 403 and a reCAPTCHA bot-check page respectively, confirmed again on retry) and were not read.

Decannulation procedure, speaking valves, cuff deflation and tube-change technique, and paediatric care: not drafted (step-by-step procedure sections not read; the AARC CPG recommends protocol-directed weaning/decannulation exists but does not itself give the steps).
Open RN via NCBI and the eCampusOntario open textbook returned browser-verification or HTTP 403 and were not read; a workaround (direct retrieval) was attempted and still failed.
